Family Health

Palpitations around menopause: assessment, triggers and treatment choices

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A fluttering, pounding or racing heartbeat can feel unsettling during perimenopause or after periods stop. It may occur during a hot flush, but that timing does not establish the cause. The aim is to recognise urgent symptoms, describe the pattern clearly and choose care that addresses both heart health and any troublesome menopause symptoms.

Palpitations are a sensation, not a diagnosis

Palpitations mean that your heartbeat becomes unusually noticeable. It may feel fast, slow, irregular, fluttering, pounding or as though a beat has been missed or added. The sensation can be felt in the chest, neck or throat. The rhythm may be normal or abnormal; the feeling alone cannot distinguish the two.

Perimenopause is the transition in which hormone levels and menstrual patterns change. Natural menopause is usually recognised after twelve months without a period when another cause or hormonal contraception does not explain the absence. Oestrogen levels change and are lower afterward; this is not a simple switch that removes all hormone production. There is no fixed eight-to-sixteen-beat increase that defines a harmless hot-flush episode. Having episodes around a period or during pregnancy likewise does not establish the cause.

Notice accompanying symptoms without assuming a hormonal cause

Hot flushes and night sweats may occur alongside a more noticeable heartbeat. Sleep difficulties, mood changes, vaginal dryness, changes in skin or hair, memory or concentration difficulties and reduced sexual desire may also occur during the transition. People experience different combinations, and palpitations can begin before periods stop or persist afterward.

These symptoms do not prove that every heartbeat change comes from menopause. Tell a clinician about heavier or unusual bleeding between periods rather than accepting it automatically as a normal transition; bleeding after established menopause needs checking even once or in a small amount. A menopause discussion and a heart-symptom assessment can happen together.

Other causes and medicines still matter

Stress, anxiety, lack of sleep, strenuous activity, caffeine, alcohol, nicotine and recreational stimulants can be relevant. Fever or illness, iron-deficiency anaemia, an overactive thyroid, heart-valve disease or a rhythm problem such as atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia are other possibilities. Feeling anxious during an episode does not prove that anxiety caused it.

Bring all prescription and nonprescription products, including cold remedies, asthma inhalers, thyroid replacement and supplements. Pseudoephedrine can cause palpitations; thyroid medicine may need a dose and blood-test review. Low glucose can cause a racing heart, especially with insulin or some diabetes medicines; follow your agreed hypo plan if this applies. Dizziness on standing may call for a blood-pressure check. Neither sugar nor extra water is a universal treatment, and you should not stop essential medicines independently. Dehydration can also be relevant; a fast heart rate with signs of dehydration needs urgent assessment.

Decide the urgency before keeping a diary

Seek immediate emergency help if palpitations are happening now and do not go away, or if they occur with chest pain or tightness, shortness of breath, dizziness or feeling faint, fainting or loss of consciousness. Do not wait for a hot flush to end, a watch reading or a menopause appointment. Do not drive yourself. If these warning symptoms have stopped, still obtain urgent medical advice the same day.

If you otherwise feel well, arrange a review when palpitations recur, become more frequent, last longer than a few minutes or worry you, and mention any personal or family heart history. An isolated brief episode may be less concerning, but duration alone cannot establish safety. A new or changing pattern deserves attention rather than a promise that it will settle once menopause is over.

Describe the pattern and start with an appropriate assessment

Note when episodes began, how long they last, whether they start and stop suddenly, and whether the heartbeat feels regular or irregular. Record any hot flush, activity, standing, stress, medicine change, pain, breathlessness or faintness. A short account is enough; do not delay urgent care or repeatedly provoke symptoms to obtain a record.

The clinician may check your pulse, blood pressure, heart sounds and general health and choose blood tests for a suspected contributor, such as anaemia or thyroid disease. An ECG records electrical activity through skin electrodes. A short resting ECG is useful but may miss an intermittent problem, so an initially normal recording does not automatically explain ongoing symptoms.

Longer monitors, scans and hormone tests answer different questions

A portable ECG or Holter monitor records over time. An event recorder or another longer monitor may be chosen when episodes are less frequent; the duration and recording method should match the pattern. An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to assess structure and function. A supervised exercise test may be useful for selected questions, with walking, cycling or an alternative when appropriate. These are options, not a package everyone must undergo.

Menopause assessment is also individual. In otherwise healthy people aged 45 or over with typical symptoms, it is usually a clinical diagnosis without routine hormone blood tests. Younger age, uncertainty, other conditions or hormonal contraception can change the approach. A hormone result does not replace investigating a concerning heartbeat, and cardiology or menopause expertise may be needed according to the findings.

Try manageable trigger changes and stress support

If no urgent feature is present, a brief diary may show that caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol, nicotine, a particular cold medicine or a food repeatedly brings on symptoms. Change one relevant factor at a time rather than banning all chocolate, spicy food or enjoyable activities. Ask a pharmacist about a suspected medicine trigger instead of changing prescribed treatment yourself.

Rest, regular sleep and gentle relaxation may help with stress. Comfortable breathing, suitable yoga or a quiet activity can be personal support; none proves the rhythm is normal or substitutes for care. Build activity gradually according to your health. Stop and seek help if exercise brings chest pain, unusual breathlessness, faintness or persistent palpitations rather than pushing through a fixed daily target.

Treat the cause and discuss menopause care separately

Some palpitations need reassurance and follow-up once assessed; others need treatment for anaemia, thyroid disease or a diagnosed heart condition. A clinician may use a beta blocker, an appropriate calcium-channel blocker or another treatment for a particular rhythm problem. These medicines are not interchangeable remedies for every menopausal flutter, and should not be started, shared or adjusted on your own.

If hot flushes, sleep disruption or other menopause symptoms affect life, discuss suitable treatment as well. HRT can help relevant menopause symptoms, but is not a diagnostic test or a replacement for treating an arrhythmia. Benefits and risks depend on age, medical history, formulation and route; oral and transdermal products do not have identical clot or stroke risks, and combined and oestrogen-only treatment differ. Menopause-specific CBT and nonhormonal options may fit some people. Do not start HRT solely to prevent cardiovascular disease, and remember that it is not contraception.

Duration and research cannot predict your individual outcome

Some people notice improvement as menopause symptoms change, while others continue to have palpitations. There is no reliable personal deadline for returning to a particular rhythm. Persistent symptoms need follow-up even after periods have stopped or an earlier test was reassuring.

Palpitations alone do not diagnose blocked arteries. A longitudinal SWAN analysis found that reported palpitation patterns were not associated with its measures of atherosclerosis or arterial stiffness after adjustment. This observational finding does not rule out a rhythm disorder or heart disease in an individual. Menopause-related and age-related cardiovascular changes still justify reviewing personal risk factors rather than assuming that either every flutter means damage or every menopausal episode is harmless.

Protect heart health and agree on follow-up

Discuss blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking and other relevant risks with your care team. Varied meals with vegetables, fruit, whole grains, appropriate protein and fats, suitable activity and smoking-cessation support can protect general health. Weight goals should be individual, and a healthy routine does not guarantee that palpitations disappear or replace indicated medicine.

Agree on what to record, when to review the results and what to do if symptoms recur. Bring a medicine list and ask what each test or treatment is intended to answer. Seek reassessment for a changing pattern; ongoing palpitations or chest, breathing, dizziness or fainting warnings require the urgent response described above even if you also have familiar hot flushes.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Check warning symptoms first; use emergency care for ongoing palpitations or associated chest, breathing, dizziness or fainting symptoms and urgent same-day advice if these have resolved.

Bring a brief symptom and medicine record; ask which ECG, monitor, blood test or scan answers the clinical question.

Discuss menopause symptoms and cardiovascular risk individually; keep follow-up and use prescribed treatments for their specific purpose.

How BeMama can help

A short note linking an episode to its duration, hot flushes, activity and medicines can help an appointment. BeMama cannot identify an arrhythmia, interpret an ECG or decide that a symptom is hormonal. Recording must never delay urgent care.

When to seek help

Seek immediate emergency help for ongoing palpitations that do not go away, or palpitations with chest pain or tightness, shortness of breath, dizziness, feeling faint, fainting or loss of consciousness; do not drive yourself. If these warning symptoms have stopped, get urgent advice the same day. Recurrent or changing episodes still need assessment. Do not independently start or stop heart, thyroid or hormone medicines.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A noticeable heartbeat can occur around menopause, but its sensation and timing do not identify the cause.
  • Ongoing palpitations or associated chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness, faintness or loss of consciousness need immediate emergency help; resolved warning episodes still need urgent same-day advice.
  • Tests are selected for the symptom pattern; not everyone needs every scan, monitor or hormone test.
  • Review medicines and personal triggers without abruptly stopping prescriptions or treating every episode with sugar, water or relaxation.
  • Menopause treatment and heart treatment need individual decisions; HRT is neither an arrhythmia remedy nor cardiovascular prevention.

Frequently asked questions

What can I do to reduce palpitations?

After checking the urgency and arranging assessment where needed, look for repeatable triggers such as caffeine, alcohol, nicotine or a medicine. Sleep and stress support may help. Do not replace testing with dietary bans or stop prescriptions yourself; treatment depends on the cause.

Will they stop after menopause?

They may improve, persist or change. No timetable guarantees that your heart symptoms will disappear. Keep follow-up for recurrent or troublesome episodes, and do not dismiss a new pattern simply because periods have stopped.

When is it an emergency?

Get emergency help now for palpitations that do not go away, or palpitations with chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, feeling faint, fainting or loss of consciousness. Do not drive yourself. If those warning symptoms have stopped, obtain urgent advice the same day rather than waiting for another episode.

Why might menopause be associated with palpitations?

Hormonal changes, hot flushes, sleep disturbance and stress can overlap with heartbeat awareness. This association does not prove that a particular episode is hormonal, does not require a fixed pulse increase and does not exclude a heart rhythm or another medical problem.

Do I need all the heart tests listed online?

No. History, examination and often an ECG guide which other tests may help. Monitoring duration depends on how often episodes occur, and ultrasound or exercise testing is chosen for a particular question. Ask why each test is recommended.

Will a hormone blood test show whether the palpitations are safe?

No. Typical menopause in otherwise healthy people aged 45 or over is usually identified clinically. Some circumstances require other tests, but a hormone result does not establish the cause or safety of an abnormal-feeling heartbeat.

Should I take HRT or a heart medicine?

Discuss separate goals with the clinician: relief of troublesome menopause symptoms, and treatment of any identified heart problem. HRT does not replace rhythm assessment or prevent cardiovascular disease as a prescribing goal. Heart medicines require a specific indication; do not self-prescribe or share them.

Does having palpitations mean I have artery disease?

Not by itself. Symptom patterns and cardiovascular research do not diagnose an individual. Review your personal risks and associated symptoms, and follow the assessment plan rather than assuming either artery damage or automatic hormonal reassurance.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
